title: The one who stopped
hook: Angulimala's song: whoever was careless and now is not lights up the world like the moon (Theragatha, Angulimala)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sunita the flower-sweeper, bowed to at dawn by gods. Your line was once despised. Did you thank someone whose work goes unseen? Today, a man who wasn't looked down on. He was feared. Day eight hundred one.

I have stopped. You stop too. In the old story, those are the Buddha's words to a man running after him with a sword. The man is Angulimala, the bandit named for the garland of fingers he wore. In the sutta he runs as hard as he can and still can't catch up, though the Buddha is only walking. He shouts at him to stop, and gets that answer back. The story of the chase is told in the Middle Length Discourses. Today we hear something else: the song the Theragatha gives to Angulimala himself, after he stopped.
screen: `I HAVE STOPPED. YOU STOP TOO.` → `HE RUNS AND CAN'T CATCH UP.` → `TODAY, HIS OWN SONG.`

segments.voice: First, his name. In his verses he says it plainly. My name was Harmless, even while I was harming. Now the name is true. I harm no one. The old name had been false. Now it fits. Second, the turn. He looks back on himself as a bandit, swept along like something in a flood, and says he went to the Buddha for refuge. He doesn't dress it up. Third, the line he's remembered for. Whoever was careless before, and afterward is not, lights up the world like the moon set free from a cloud. The same verse stands in the Dhammapada, and Max Müller's old translation gives it like this: "He who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." Notice what the picture keeps. The clouds were real. The moon doesn't pretend they weren't there. It comes out from behind them. Fourth, the cost. In the sutta, after he becomes a monk, Angulimala goes for alms and people throw clods and stones. He comes back bleeding, his bowl broken, his robe torn. And the Buddha tells him to bear it: the fruit of what he did is ripening now, here. So the moon from the cloud isn't a clean slate. It's a turning point, and then a road. Some readers ask whether the story comes too easily, and what of the people he hurt. The text doesn't hide from that. It keeps the light and the stones in the same story.
screen: `HARMLESS: NOW THE NAME IS TRUE.` · `SWEPT ALONG, THEN TAKING REFUGE.` · `THE MOON SET FREE FROM A CLOUD.` · `STONES ON THE ALMS ROUND.` · then, large: `THE MOON FROM THE CLOUD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: begin again today. Sit, and let one thing come to mind that you'd like to have done differently. Not the worst thing. Something recent and ordinary. A sharp word. A promise you dropped. Don't pretend it didn't happen; the clouds were real. Just stop, the way Angulimala stopped. Then, on an out-breath, let a small next step show itself: an apology, a call, doing it better tomorrow. You don't have to take it yet. Just let it come into view, like the moon coming out. The bell holds the time.
The one who stopped. Angulimala: the bandit who stopped running, became a monk, and sang of the moon set free from a cloud. Today's word.
Your line: the moon from the cloud. Today, take the one small next step you saw, and let it be a beginning, not a fix. Day eight hundred one.

howItsDone: In some Theravada countries, monks chant the Angulimala paritta, a protective verse from his story, for women in childbirth, and teachers tell his story when they speak of beginning again.

original.note: Pali: anguli, finger, and mala, garland. The name he carried as a bandit.

trapdoor: what you thought: a bad man made good overnight.
what it means: Angulimala's song: whoever turns from carelessness lights up the world like the moon from a cloud, and the stones still come.
what a scholar hears: his verses play on his given name, Harmless (Ahimsaka), and the moon verse also stands in the Dhammapada.

sources.quoted: He who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds.

notes: Quoted Dhammapada 172 from Max Müller (1881), checked from memory; please verify word for word.
Thag 16.8 paraphrased: the name Ahimsaka ('Harmless') once false, now true; swept along as by a flood, he took refuge; the moon verse (shared with Dhp 172). Confirm.

MN 86 paraphrased: 'I have stopped, Angulimala; you stop too'; he cannot catch the walking Buddha; struck by clods and stones on alms round, bowl broken, robe torn; the Buddha tells him to bear it as the ripening of his deeds here and now. Confirm.
The finger-garland meaning of the name is the plain meaning given in the sutta's story; confirm.
